anchor: anti-luminosity: roughly, the assumption that whenever a condition obtains, one is automatically in a position to know that it obtains. His argument uses reliability, limited discrimination and sorites-style reasoning. ... EvidenceExists(e) not=> EvaluatorCanEstablish(EvidenceExists(e)) ... Zero(K)=0 not=> Known(Zero(K)=0). anchor: Cases in which p is known can be separated from cases in which p is false by a buffer of true-but-unknown cases. ... Known(p)\Rightarrow Margin(p,\Gamma)>0 ... the required margin can vary from point to point and need not be uniform ... Margin \neq Confidence ... Epistemic quality \neq scalar score

anchor: two conditions for e to count as evidence for h: 1. e must speak in favor of h; 2. e must have appropriate epistemic standing. ... Evidence = Support + Standing ... whether evidence e raises the probability of h depends on background information ... Evidence(e,h)=f(Support(e,h),Standing(e),Context(Gamma))

anchor: knowledge first ... the simple distinction between knowledge and ignorance as a starting point ... Knowledge \neq True Belief + X (No non-circular specification of X) ... Knowing is the most general factive stative attitude ... FMSO: Factive, Stative, Propositional, Unanalysable
statement: States the knowledge-first primitivism thesis (knowledge is not analysable into belief+truth+justification, via failed-Gettier-analysis and a coloured/red analogy) and formally defines the Factive Mental State Operator (FMSO: factive, stative, propositional, unanalysable) with the inference rule 'if Phi is an FMSO, from S-Phis-that-A one may infer S-knows-that-A'; translated as K_t should be represented as a mental state of the knower, not merely stored propositions, and treated as a primitive status.

anchor: Desire | Mind->World | aspires to action ... Belief | Mind->World | aspires to truth ... Knowledge | World->Mind | satisfies belief ... Belief aims at Knowledge just as Desire aims at Action. Knowledge is the success condition for belief.
statement: Direction-of-fit table analogy: Desire:Action (mind->world:world->mind) parallels Belief:Knowledge, with Knowledge as the success condition for Belief just as Action is the success condition for Desire.

anchor: One's total evidence is simply one's total knowledge. ... A false proposition cannot be evidence, even if it is justifiedly believed. ... Sat(K_t,r) requires knowledge, not just true belief ... Provenance must track whether a claim is known or merely believed.
statement: The unhedged Evidence=Knowledge thesis (a false, even justifiedly-believed, proposition cannot be evidence) translated directly: Sat(K_t,r) requires knowledge not true belief, Boundary should distinguish known from merely-believed, Provenance must track known-vs-believed.

anchor: The regress of justification ends at knowledge. ... One's belief is justified absolutely if and only if it is justified relative to one's knowledge. ... K_t is the foundation ... Determination should be grounded in knowledge, not in infinite regress
statement: Regress-of-justification argument (justification chains must terminate somewhere; they terminate at knowledge) translated as: K_t (knowledge state) is the foundation of the justification chain, and Determination should be grounded in K_t rather than an infinite regress.

anchor: we do not know that the ticket did not win. Beliefs based on such probabilistic evidence are not knowledge. ... high probability \neq knowledge ... Sat(K_t,r) cannot be satisfied by probability alone.
statement: The lottery-ticket example (999,999/1,000,000 true belief the ticket lost is still not knowledge) argues high probability != knowledge, translated as Sat(K_t,r) cannot be satisfied by probability/probabilistic support alone -- must distinguish probabilistic support from knowledge/certainty.

anchor: A condition C is defined to be luminous if and only if: For every case alpha, if in alpha C obtains, then in alpha one is in a position to know that C obtains. ... The Sorites-Style Argument [feeling cold at dawn to hot at noon] ... Therefore the condition 'one feels cold' is not luminous.
statement: Gives the formal definition of luminosity (a condition C is luminous iff whenever C obtains one is in a position to know it obtains) and the full sorites-style anti-luminosity argument (feeling-cold-at-dawn-to-hot-at-noon, imperceptible per-step changes) proving virtually no mental state is luminous, including love/hope examples generalizing beyond feeling-cold; grounds the epistemic-non-transparency principle with its original formal source material.

anchor: if we combine the argument with the principle that one is always in a position to know what one's evidence is, the upshot is that one has exactly the same evidence in an ordinary case and its sceptical counterpart. ... Luminous conditions are trivial. Since mental states are non-luminous, the sceptical argument fails. ... KnowledgeOS should not adopt a phenomenal conception of evidence.
statement: Uses non-luminosity to dissolve philosophical scepticism (if evidence were luminous, evidence would be identical between ordinary and sceptical cases, but mental states are non-luminous so the argument fails) and explicitly rejects the phenomenal conception of evidence (a converging-to-the-empty-set sequence of ever-more-private appearances), translated as: KnowledgeOS's evidence must not be modeled as private/phenomenal appearances.

anchor: Mr Magoo sees a tree ... he cannot know for any i that the tree is not i inches tall ... Therefore, KK (knowledge that one knows) fails. ... Further iterations of knowledge are even harder to achieve.
statement: The Mr-Magoo margin-for-error argument formally derives the failure of the KK principle (knowledge does not imply knowledge of knowledge) via a step-by-step discrimination-limit argument, and notes iterations beyond the second are progressively harder to achieve -- the original formal source for the epistemic-iteration-non-closure principle.

anchor: just as one cannot always know what one's evidence is, so one cannot always know what rationality requires of one. ... rationality is not luminous. ... the system cannot assume that Determination is always accessible.
statement: Extends non-luminosity specifically to rationality (one cannot always know what rationality requires), translated as: KnowledgeOS cannot assume Determination is always accessible/transparent to the system itself.

anchor: If something is an unknown truth, then that it is an unknown truth is itself an unknowable truth. ... K(p\land\neg Kp)\supset(Kp\land K\neg Kp) ... all truths are knowable, then all truths are known. Since not all truths are known, not all truths are knowable. ... It is impossible to know that p is true and unknown. ... A gap cannot be known as a gap. Zero cannot be known as Zero.
statement: Full five-step formal Fitch's-paradox derivation (knowledge distributes over conjunction; factivity; no one can know an unknown truth; weak verificationism that all truths are knowable; therefore not all truths are knowable, since not all truths are known) plus the Moorean-twist corollary (impossible to know p-is-true-and-unknown); translated as: a Gap cannot be known AS a gap, Zero cannot be known AS Zero, Boundaries cannot be fully known -- a structural limit on KnowledgeOS's own self-representation of its unknowns.

assumptions.statement: weak verificationism (all truths are knowable) is assumed for the paradox's derivation, not asserted as a KnowledgeOS commitment

anchor: The fundamental rule of assertion is that one should assert p only if one knows p. ... explains why lottery assertions are inappropriate ... explains Moore's paradox ... explains the challenge "How do you know?" ... Assert in KnowledgeOS should be governed by a knowledge rule.
statement: States the Knowledge Rule of assertion (assert p only if you know p) and its explanatory power (lottery-assertion inappropriateness, Moore's paradox, the 'how do you know?' challenge), translated as: KnowledgeOS's Assert operation should be governed by a knowledge rule rather than a mere-truth or mere-belief rule -- a stronger, unhedged version of the later assertion-responsibility candidate in S2528.

anchor: World -> Perception -> Knowledge -> Evidence -> Justification -> Belief -> Assertion -> Action ... World -> Observation -> K_t (Knowledge State) -> Evidence -> Sat -> Determination -> Decision -> Action -> K_{t+1}
statement: Translates Williamson's implied epistemic pipeline (World->Perception->Knowledge->Evidence->Justification->Belief->Assertion->Action) into a KnowledgeOS pipeline World->Observation->K_t->Evidence->Sat->Determination->Decision->Action->K_{t+1}, notably placing Evidence AFTER K_t and treating Sat as directly consuming Evidence -- a less hedged pipeline than the Representation->Reasoning->Evaluation->Determination pipelines proposed in the DL/Situation-Calculus threads.

anchor: What to Adopt: Knowledge First ✅ ... Evidence = Knowledge ✅ ... Factive Mental States ✅ ... Non-Luminosity ✅ ... Margin for Error ✅ ... Anti-KK ✅ ... Knowledge Rule for Assertion ✅ ... What to Reject: Knowledge = Justified True Belief ❌ ... Phenomenal Evidence ❌ ... Transparency of Rationality ❌ ... Luminosity of Mental States ❌ ... statement: Final recommendation table adopts all seven listed concepts (Knowledge First, Evidence=Knowledge, Factive Mental States, Non-Luminosity, Margin for Error, Anti-KK, Knowledge Rule for Assertion) unconditionally (all checked, no [PROP]/[OPEN] hedging) and recommends integrating them directly into KnowledgeOS Theory v1.2 -- a materially stronger, less-hedged recommendation than the same-day review (S2528), which instead treats most of these as PROP-status research candidates and explicitly places 'Evidence=Knowledge' on its own rejection list.
